value.text: On February 11, 2025, Vice President Vance described AI as exceptionally promising across economic innovation, employment, national security, health care, and free expression. In the same speech, he advocated worker-centered policies to secure productivity and prosperity gains and prioritized AI opportunities while acknowledging safety concerns. In September and October 2026, he called for AI companies to build safe tools and take responsibility for harms they warn their technology could cause.

In the same speech, he advocated worker-centered policies to secure productivity and prosperity gains and prioritized AI opportunities while acknowledging safety concerns.
In September and October 2026, he called for AI companies to build safe tools and take responsibility for harms they warn their technology could cause.

value.reason: The clearest general assessments are opportunity-oriented statements from February 11, 2025; several are excerpts from the same speech, not independent occasions. The remaining evidence concerns particular risks, worker participation, regulation, infrastructure, or announcements without establishing an overall benefit-harm judgment. Supplied source context resolves the relevant truncated passages, but these findings do not establish that the February 2025 outlook remained unchanged in later statements.

He also stated that AI governance must be local and that the United States totally rejects global governance of AI.

value.text: In April 2024, PCAST recommended that federal funding agencies consider requiring responsible AI use plans from researchers and updating data management plan requirements to disclose AI tools used in proposed research. PCAST also strongly encouraged expanding pilot programs for secure data access and developing federal database management guidelines that incorporate privacy protection technologies. PCAST recommended that the NAIRR pilot be expeditiously expanded to the scale envisioned by the NAIRR Task Force and fully funded. PCAST described AI as having great potential to accelerate science and technology for societal benefit and to help address challenges such as human health and weather prediction.

value.text: In 2023 congressional testimony, Paul Dabbar said Chinese hardware and AI algorithms could pose national security risks and recommended banning all chips, software, electric vehicle components, and power grid controls from China. In May 2025 hearing statements, he said broad AI regulation could impede economic progress and that NIST should focus on traditional strengths such as standards and measurement. In December 2025 official-role remarks and a January 2026 reported statement, he said AI can increase manufacturer competitiveness and attract investment in America.

value.text: In a March 2026 Senate opening statement, Raman said that if confirmed he would help NIST deliver on the President’s AI action plan and maximize innovation across the American AI tech stack, including semiconductors, quantum, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing. In the same statement, he described a vision for NIST focused on accelerating technology innovation through industry partnerships, championing trusted technology standards globally, and speeding adoption by American industry. In 2024 reported statements from Purdue, he cited an urgent need for AI-equipped sensor networks to detect and identify threats and noted the Institute of Chips and AI among Purdue programs focused on physical AI. In August 2026 as NIST Director, Raman said NIST’s contribution to the Genesis Mission reflected its commitment to U.S. leadership in critical technologies and that NIST was using public-private partnerships to apply advanced AI to manufacturing and cybersecurity.

sentences.text: In a March 2026 Senate opening statement, Raman said that if confirmed he would help NIST deliver on the President’s AI action plan and maximize innovation across the American AI tech stack, including semiconductors, quantum, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing.

In the same statement, he described a vision for NIST focused on accelerating technology innovation through industry partnerships, championing trusted technology standards globally, and speeding adoption by American industry.

In 2024 reported statements from Purdue, he cited an urgent need for AI-equipped sensor networks to detect and identify threats and noted the Institute of Chips and AI among Purdue programs focused on physical AI.

In August 2026 as NIST Director, Raman said NIST’s contribution to the Genesis Mission reflected its commitment to U.S. leadership in critical technologies and that NIST was using public-private partnerships to apply advanced AI to manufacturing and cybersecurity.

value.reason: The supplied excerpts express enthusiasm for AI innovation, describe research programs and specific applications, or promote technology leadership generally. None establishes a view of AI’s overall effects on Americans. This conclusion is limited to the supplied excerpts, not Raman’s views elsewhere.

value.text: In May 2026, Deputy NIST Director Craig Burkhardt invited technically capable organizations to join the NIST AI Consortium and said NIST was seeking to expand AI measurement efforts by harnessing the broader community’s interests and capabilities. In March 2026, he said the CAISI-GSA partnership would enable federal agencies to adopt AI in ways that help the American people and expressed excitement about advancing AI in support of the Trump Administration’s innovation vision. In December 2025, while Acting NIST Director, he said his goal was to remove barriers to American AI innovation and accelerate the application of AI technologies around the world. Also in December 2025, he described a new MITRE agreement as focused on helping U.S. companies make high-value products more efficiently, meet market demands, and catalyze discovery and commercialization of new technologies and devices.

sentences.text: In May 2026, Deputy NIST Director Craig Burkhardt invited technically capable organizations to join the NIST AI Consortium and said NIST was seeking to expand AI measurement efforts by harnessing the broader community’s interests and capabilities.

In March 2026, he said the CAISI-GSA partnership would enable federal agencies to adopt AI in ways that help the American people and expressed excitement about advancing AI in support of the Trump Administration’s innovation vision.
In December 2025, while Acting NIST Director, he said his goal was to remove barriers to American AI innovation and accelerate the application of AI technologies around the world.

Also in December 2025, he described a new MITRE agreement as focused on helping U.S. companies make high-value products more efficiently, meet market demands, and catalyze discovery and commercialization of new technologies and devices.

He has also advocated a pro-innovation, pro-growth approach to AI and argued that AI will create jobs and growth rather than suppress workers.

value.text: In June 2026 remarks at an Amazon Web Services summit, CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the agency’s new Acquisition Framework and Procurement Executive aim to complete most acquisitions within six months. He described frontier AI models as potentially akin to “digital nuclear weapons” and said he made emerging technologies a top priority alongside China. Ratcliffe argued that the CIA cannot wait for a risk-free approach to emerging technology, must move fast and aggressively, and must master it better than adversaries. He said widespread AI adoption is transforming the agency’s work and that adversaries seek to steal and manipulate America’s advancements.

value.text: As EPA Administrator, Lee Zeldin repeatedly stated his goal for the United States to become the "AI capital of the world" and described EPA's role in permitting reform and regulatory streamlining to support AI infrastructure and data centers. He linked AI development to energy policy, saying America must win the global AI race while working families should not have to pay for it, and he referenced the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. He criticized a New York statewide moratorium on data centers in the context of U.S. AI competition and cited an Energy Information Administration projection that electricity demand from AI-supporting data centers will rise substantially.
